cards.say: Governance isn't about slowing AI down. It's about knowing which uses need a light touch, and which need real oversight, before something goes wrong.

cards.q: Match the AI use to its rough risk level
pairs: Low: a person reads it before it goes anywhere
High: it directly affects someone's rights
Low: mistakes are cheap and easy to catch
High: it can systematically exclude people
cards.why: Risk depends on what happens if it's wrong and who it affects, not on how advanced the technology is.

cards.q: Which control matters most for a high-risk use, like a hiring or lending decision?
options: A human review step and a way to audit outcomes
cards.why: For decisions that affect people's lives, oversight and the ability to audit outcomes matter more than raw model quality.

cards.q: Myth or fact: one AI policy document is enough to manage AI risk across a company.
cards.why: A policy sets expectations, but risk still needs a case-by-case look, since a chatbot FAQ and an automated approval system carry very different risk.

cards.q: One of these governance habits backfires. Tap it.
sentences: Review high-risk use cases before they launch, not after.
Route every low-risk internal draft through a formal review board.
Keep a record of what data informed each system.
cards.why: Heavy review on low-risk work slows teams down without cutting real risk, and it teaches people to route around governance entirely. Save the heavy process for what actually needs it.

cards.why: Match the process to the stakes. Light review for low-stakes work, real oversight for anything that can seriously hurt someone if it's wrong.
